claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a supersaturated FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy contains fine incipient nitride precipitates at grain boundaries or triple junctions.
The as-built alloy contains fine incipient sigma-phase precipitates at grain boundaries or triple junctions.
Prolonged exposure at approximately 900–1300 K causes Cr-rich sigma-phase precipitates to grow or coarsen preferentially at grain boundaries.
Prolonged exposure at approximately 900–1300 K causes Cr-rich nitride precipitates to form and coarsen preferentially at grain boundaries.
Elevated-temperature precipitation and coarsening are accelerated by atomic diffusion from the supersaturated as-built matrix.
Grain-boundary precipitates reduce intergranular cohesive strength.
Loss of grain-boundary cohesion enables crack nucleation and rapid intergranular fracture under thermal or mechanical load.
Secondary-phase precipitation in FCC high-entropy alloys can substantially alter mechanical properties and can cause embrittlement.
Sigma phase begins to enlarge and preferentially occupy grain boundaries at about 950 K.
Sigma-phase evolution at grain boundaries can significantly reduce mechanical and chemical properties.
Increasing nitrogen availability or using air will increase the density and size of grain-boundary Cr-rich nitride and sigma-phase precipitates relative to a low-nitrogen atmosphere.
A low-nitrogen, inert, or reducing atmosphere will suppress nitride and sigma-phase precipitation.
Standard nitrogen-containing exposure will produce lower microhardness and tensile ductility than low-nitrogen exposure.
Standard nitrogen-containing exposure will cause more intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure than low-nitrogen exposure.
Below approximately 900 K, diffusion is too slow for the proposed degradation mechanism to apply.
Two otherwise identical specimen sets can be compared after 200 hours at the same temperature under standard-nitrogen and calibrated low-nitrogen atmospheres.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says exposure in either oxidizing or reducing gas accelerates the proposed precipitation, while the conditions treat an inert/reducing gas mixture as the modified atmosphere expected to minimize precipitation and degradation.

The baseline is defined alternatively as the unexposed as-built state or as a thermally exposed low-nitrogen state, although these are not equivalent starting-state baselines and may have different thermally driven microstructures.
